# The register rules: Reginn

The internet spells **Reginn** more ways than one, and only one of them is the name the sources wrote. This is the register's ruling — canonical, fallback, contested, and false, each in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Reginn
- **Original script:** ᚱᛁᚴᛁᚾᚾ
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Convention:** normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 336 of 437

## The Canonical Form

The attested form is **ᚱᛁᚴᛁᚾᚾ**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Reginn**.

No diacritics are required here: the canonical form is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them demands.

## Where the Flattened Form Stands

The plain form *reginn* differs from the canonical **Reginn** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

## The Register of False Forms

No circulating form of this name currently qualifies as false under the register's standard — a rare standing. The spelling is short, sturdy, and rarely mangled.

## The Contested Forms

No alternate form of this name carries documented scholarly support in the lexicon's record. The convention here — normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them — produces exactly one defensible transliteration: **Reginn**. Forms that differ from it are not contested; they are simply wrong.

## The Convention's Own History

Old Norse orthography is a primary source in itself: þ (thorn) and ð (eth) are letters the language used natively, not transliteration marks — English once had them too, and lost them. ǫ (o with ogonek) is a nasal vowel with its own saga-era history, and normalized Old Norse spelling preserves it because the Eddas' editors do. To write th for þ or o for ǫ is not modernization; it is a different spelling of a different word. The Eddic poems survive in one manuscript tradition each — the register spells the names the way those manuscripts do.

## What the Address Bar Allows

IDNA 2008 permits the letters these restorations use — macrons, acutes, underdots, thorn, ogonek, the lot — and the DNS carries them as punycode (`xn--` labels). Two honest constraints remain. First, **registrar inventory**: the protocol permits a character; the registrar's stock decides whether the exact domain can be bought today. Second, **combined marks**: forms like *Apṓllōn* (acute stacked on a macron) are philologically ideal yet effectively untypeable on phones and unsupported across much of the registration system.

That is why the rulebook keeps a fallback hierarchy — full restoration first, then the circumflex when the source carries one, then the macron-only academic standard, then an attested variant, and only as a last resort the plain ASCII form. **Every step down the ladder is still defensible; nothing on the ladder is a wrong mark.** A fallback is a choice among attested forms. A false form is not on the ladder at all.

## Where the Name Stood First

Reginn is a textual figure, but the Völsung cycle is among the most picture-rich narratives in the North, and the smith's scenes were carved. The great Sigurðr iconography of Viking-Age Scandinavia — the carving of the dragon-slaying, the heart-roasting, and the listening to birds — survives on the Swedish runestones at Ramsund (Sö 101) and Gök (Sö 327) in Södermanland, on the Drävle stone (U 1163) in Uppland, and on the Manx crosses at Jurby, Malew and Andreas, where the roasting scene and Sigurðr's thumb in his mouth are unmistakable. The Ramsund carving shows the full cycle's cast: the slain Fáfnir as a serpent-band, Sigurðr at the fire, the horse Grani loaded with the hoard, the birds in the tree — and the headless smith's tools laid beside a headless body, the standard scholarly reading of the truncated figure at the carving's edge as the killed Reginn. In England, the Halton cross in Lancashire and the York Minster grave slab carry related scenes. The manuscript witnesses are the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (Reginsmál, Fáfnismál), the codices of Snorri's Edda for Skáldskaparmál's prose account, and the vellum of Völsunga saga (AM 182 4to and the paper tradition) for the fullest prose life. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Verdict

The register rules for **Reginn**, and the ruling is checkable: every mark sourced, every violation stated, every borderline form given its honest standing. *reginn* carries the name freely — it differs only in display, and the register says so without reservation. Anything else in circulation has its origin and its failure recorded above. That is the whole of the law on this name — and the temple at [/reginn/](/reginn/) enforces it.

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 6 cited sources — Poetic Edda: Reginsmál (prose and stanzas: the fosterage; the gold's history), Fáfnismál (the dragon's warnings; the nuthatches; the killing of Reginn); Völuspá 12 (Reginn in the catalogue of dwarfs), trans. Carolyne Larrington, Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál (the otter's ransom; Andvari's gold and Andvaranautr; the curse; Fáfnir's parricide and Reginn's exclusion), trans. Anthony Faulkes, Völsunga saga, chs. 13–20 (Reginn at Hjálprek's court; the fosterage; the reforging of Gram from Sigmundr's shards; the death of Fáfnir and of Reginn), trans. Jesse L. Byock.
